title: "Time in rocks"
---

## Introduction

This chapter introduces the concept of **age-depth models**, which formalize geochronological knowledge and contain a lot of stratigraphic information, e.g., on sediment accumulation rates and hiatus location and duration.

At the end of the chapter you will

* be able to explain what an age-depth model is and what stratigraphic information it contains
* have an intuition on how age-depth models modify the stratigraphic distribution of fossils

These materials are adopted form the workshop "[Modeling Stratigraphic Paleobiology in R](https://mindthegap-erc.github.io/StratPal_workshop_materials/)".

## Tasks and discussion points

1. Work through the materials to get a feeling for how age-depth models work, which stratigraphic information they contain, and how they shape the stratigraphic distribution of fossils.

2. Explore the spatial variability of the age-depth models. What changes most/least, and how does this propagate into paleontological and evolutionary interpretations?

Of course you can replace the example data provided by the data you generated using CarboKitten. Does this change results? For both tasks above, pay attention to the connection between the external forcing (eustatic sea level and subsidence) and the observed biases. Do you see a connection or not? Does this change spatially?

For your own study system (studied group and temporal and spatial scale of observation), where do your age-depth models come from? Are you aware of them, or do you use them implicitly?

## What are age-depth models

Age-depth models are formalizations of geochronological and stratigraphic knowledge: For a given stratigraphic position, they allow us to determine the age/time of deposition, and for any age/time, they determine the stratigraphic position formed at that point in time. They are models in the sense that we usually don't know them perfectly, but have to estimate them from data such as from radioisotope data and biostratigraphic information.

Broadly, everything that translates data between the *time domain* (time dimension, SI units seconds and derived units such as Myr) and the *stratigraphic domain* (length/position dimension, SI units m and derived units) is an age model. So if you find a fossil somewhere in an outcrop and say "This fossil is approx. 37 Ma old" you have applied an age-depth model, even only implicitly and using many mental shortcuts. Conversely, if you run a stratigraphic model and say "after 2 Myr elapsed model time, the model has accumulated 73 m of sediment", you are also using an age-depth model. Notably, the age-depth models we will be using are usually **not parametric** in the sense that they can be easily described by a small number of parameters, but are quite messy as they are results of complex physical and biological processes such as sediment transport and spatial dispersal and competition of organisms.

## Loading data and constructing age-depth models

First let's load the data from your stratigraphic forward model:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
adm_name = "data/output/columns_adm.csv" # adjust if you have a different output location
data_adm = read.csv(adm_name) # read age-depth model data
```
:::


For the time being, we focus on one specific location in the simulated platform, namely the proximal section. We start by extracting the time steps and the height data at the examined location. Here we use the section that we named the "proximal" in the CarboKitten example. Of course you can always change which section you examine by changing the key or by importing a specific column from the data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
key = "proximal"
t =  data_adm[,which(grepl("Myr",names(data_adm)))] # time step
h = data_adm[,which(grepl(key,names(data_adm)))] # heights at the location with key in the name
```
:::


With this, we can define the age-depth model object:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
adm = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = t,
                          h = h,
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")
adm
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
age-depth model
```


:::
:::


Here `tp_to_adm` stands for "tie points to age-depth model".

You can get a quick overview of the properties of the age-depth model using `summary`:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
age-depth model 
Total duration: 1 Myr
Total thickness: 46.0238 m
Stratigraphic completeness: 35.34 % 
39 hiatus(es)
```


:::
:::


Plotting age-depth models works out of the box using the default `plot` function. You can plot the accumulative and destructive intervals separately.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(adm,
     lwd_destr = 1, # line width destructive interval (hiatus)
     lwd_acc = 2, # line width accumulative interval
     col_destr = "blue",
     col_acc = "black")
admtools::T_axis_lab() # add time axis label
admtools::L_axis_lab() # add length axis label (stratigraphic domain)
title(main = paste("Age-depth model at ", key, "location"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/plot-age-depth-model-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

Here, gaps in the record are highlighted in blue.

## Extracting data from age-depth models

Internally, age-depth model objects are just a list of times and associated heights plus information about which intervals are erosive (meaning, they remove data). However, they are incredibly convenient to quickly extract basic stratigraphic information from.

For example, you can easily determine the number of hiatuses, time span covered, sediment accumulated, and stratigraphic (in)completeness:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# no of hiatuses
admtools::get_hiat_no(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 39
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# total duration
admtools::get_total_duration(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# total thickness of sediment accumulated
admtools::get_total_thickness(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 46.0238
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# stratigraphic (in)completeness
# note this is incompleteness on the timescale of the time steps of your forward simulation
# here on the scale of your forward simulation
admtools::get_incompleteness(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.6466
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
admtools::get_completeness(adm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.3534
```


:::
:::


You can extract more information, e.g., exact gap timing and positions, using `get_hiat_list`.

In addition, you can extract information on sediment accumulation rates, both in the temporal and stratigraphic domain:


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# constants for convenience
t_min = admtools::min_time(adm)
t_max = admtools::max_time(adm)
h_min = admtools::min_height(adm)
h_max = admtools::max_height(adm)
t_step = 0.01 # 10 kyr resolution
h_step = 1 # meter resolution
# plotting values
t_vals = seq(t_min, t_max, by = t_step)
h_vals = seq(h_min, h_max, by = h_step)
# Time domain plot
plot(x = t_vals,
     y = admtools::sed_rate_t(adm, t_vals),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Sediment accumulation rate [m/Myr]",
     main = "Sediment accumulation (Time domain)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/plot-sed-acc-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Stratigraphic domain plot
plot(x = admtools::sed_rate_l(adm, h_vals),
     y = h_vals,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Sediment accumulation [m/Myr]",
     ylab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
     main = "Sediment accumulation (Stratigraphic domain)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/plot-sed-acc-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


This nicely displays a major difference between the temporal and stratigraphic domain: In the time domain, sediment accumulation can be 0 (or even negative) during times of sedimentary stasis, stagnation, or erosion. However, in the stratigraphic domain, sediment accumulation must always be positive as only intervals with positive sediment accumulation can be preserved and make it into the sedimentary record.

For this reason, it can be more intuitive to plot *sediment condensation* instead, which is the amout of time preserved per stratigraphic increment:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(x = admtools::condensation(adm, h_vals),
     y = h_vals,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Condensation [Myr/m]",
     ylab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
     main = "Sediment condensation (Stratigraphic domain)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/plot-sedimen-condensation-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Note that this plot is still in the stratigraphic domain, but the units are Myr/m instead of m/Myr as in the sedimentation rate.

Both with sediment accumulation and condensation, keep in mind that both are extremeny sensitive to the timescale of observation. Changing the scale (`t_step` and `h_step` above) can thus drastically change your plots.

## Transforming data between the temporal and stratigraphic domain (and vice versa)

The real power of age-depth models is that they can transform data from the time domain to the stratigraphic domain and vice versa. In the `admtools` package, this is performed by two functions:

* `time_to_strat` uses an age-depth model to transform data from the time domain to the stratigraphic domain by replacing entries that reflect time by stratigraphic positions. It takes an optional argument `destructive` that specifies whether gaps act destructively (i.e., to remove data) or not
* `strat_to_time` used an age-depth model to transform data from the stratigraphic domain to the time domain by replacing entries that reflect stratigraphic position by times.

### Base case

Let's look at a simple example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# times
t_example = c(0.2, 0.5)
# transform into stratigraphic positions
h_example = admtools::time_to_strat(t_example,
                                    adm)
# display
h_example
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12.94445       NA
```


:::
:::


Here you can see that the time of 0.2 is placed at 13 m stratigraphic height, but the time at 0.5 Myr is associated with a hiatus and is "destroyed" (the argument `destructive` defaults to `TRUE`). For comparison:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
h_example = admtools::time_to_strat(t_example,
                                    adm,
                                    destructive = FALSE)
# display
h_example
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12.94445 25.49968
```


:::
:::

returns two numeric values, where 25.5 m is the stratigraphic position of the hiatal surface associated with the gap.

The transformation of data from the stratigraphic domain to the time domain works identically:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# example stratigraphic positions
h_example = c(4,30)
t_example = admtools::strat_to_time(obj = h_example,
                                    x = adm)
t_example
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.04825809 0.57217924
```


:::
:::


Here you can see that the stratigraphic position at 4 m was formed after 0.048 Myr in your simulation, and that the position at 30 m was formed after 0.57 Myr.

### Application to fossil abundance and last occurrences

The power of this conceptual approach is that it immediately generalizes to any type of temporal and stratigraphic data.

As a first example, let's first simulate fossil occurrences of a single taxon in the time domain. 

::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# set seed for reproducibility
seed = 42
set.seed(seed)
# small constant
eps = 0.01
max_rate = 1000
# fossil occurrences peak 10-fold beteen 0.5 and 0.55 Myr 
rate = approxfun(x = c(t_min, 0.45, 0.45 + eps, 0.53, 0.53 + eps, t_max),
              y = 100 * c(1, 1, 10, 10, 1, 1),
              rule = 2)
plot(x = t,
     y = rate(t),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Abundance [Fossils/Myr]",
     main = "Fossil abundance",
     ylim = c(0, max_rate))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/fossil-abundance-baseline-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sim_fossils = StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = rate,
                                    from = t_min,
                                    to = t_max,
                                    f_max = max_rate)
hist(sim_fossils,
     breaks = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 30),
    xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     main = " Simulated fossil abundance in the time domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/fossil-abundance-baseline-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now we can transform the these fossils into the stratigraphic domain:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sim_fossils_strat = sim_fossils |> 
  admtools::time_to_strat(adm)
hist(sim_fossils_strat,
     breaks = seq(h_min, h_max, length.out = 30),
     xlab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
     main = "Fossil abundance in the stratigraphic domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/fossil-abundance-stratigraphy-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Two things are notable here: First, there are very few fossils preserved in the stratigraphic domain (45 vs. 189 in the time domain) due to the destructive effect of the gaps. Second, the peak in fossil abundance is almost completely missing, as it largely coincides with a gap.

Of course the same works in the other direction: Assuming we observe a uniform fossil abundance in the stratigraphic domain, the reconstructed fossil abundance in the time domain is:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
StratPal::p3(rate = 10,
             from = h_min,
             to = h_max) |>
  admtools::strat_to_time(x = adm) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 30),
       xlab = "Time [Myr]",
       ylab = "Fossil abundance",
       main = "Reconstructed fossil abundance in time domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/fossil-abundance-time-domain-reconstructed-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Note here the gaps in fossil abundance are due to the gaps in the fossil record - no fossil ages will be reconstructed during the gap. If you want to explore the interaction between sediment accumulation, age-depth models, and fossil abundance more interactively, check out the [Shellbed condensator](https://utrecht-university.shinyapps.io/ShellbedCondensator/), a shiny app that runs in your browser.

Last, we show off a classic example of stratigraphic paleobiology: The generation of artifactual clusters of last occurrences at hiatal surfaces from fossil taxa simulated under a scenario where extinction rate increases gradually through time. This example quietly assumes that for each taxon, the fossil abundance is high enough for the Signor-Lipps effect to be negligible (Why is this assumption needed, and where is it expressed in the code?)

For the extinction rate, we assume it doubles over the timescale of observation. To reduce the effects of noise, we simulate a (unrealistically) large number of last occurrences:


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_lfo = 1000 # no of last occurrences
f_lo = approxfun(x = c(t_min, t_max),
              y = c(1,2), # double over timescale of observation
              rule = 2)
plot(x = t,
     y = f_lo(t),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Extinction rate [-]",
     main = "Extinction rate",
     yaxt = "n",
     ylim = c(0,max(f_lo(t))))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/last-occurrences-baseline-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
last_occ = StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = f_lo,
                                 from = t_min,
                                 to = t_max,
                                 n = n_lfo, # condition on the required number of last occurrences
                                 f_max = 2)
hist(last_occ,
     breaks = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 30),
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Last occurrences [#/Myr]",
     main = "Last occurrences in the time domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/last-occurrences-baseline-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now let's transfor this into the stratigraphic domain to see where the last occurrences cluster. We use the option `destructive = FALSE` to make sure the last occurrences during a gap appear directly at the stratigraphic position of the associated hiatus surface.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
last_occ |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(x = adm,
                          destructiv = FALSE) |>
  hist(breaks = seq(h_min, h_max, length.out = 30),
       xlab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
       main = "Last occurrences in the stratigraphic domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/last-occurrences-stratigraphic-domain-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Note the peaks in the histogram at stratigraphic positions with a hiatus surface. In contrast to the simulation with the fossil abundances, here the number of last occurrences is identical in the time and stratigraphic domain.

### Effects on trait evolution

As a last example, we show how age-depth models can modify our understanding of trait evolution along lineages.

As a baseline, let's simulate a trait evolving according to a random walk along a lineage:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
t_res = 0.01 # temporal resolution
t_sampled = seq(from = t_min, # times where the lineage is sampled
                to = t_max,
                by = t_res)
# model parameters
sigma = 1 # variance
mu = 3 # directionality
lineage_t = StratPal::random_walk(t = t_sampled,
                                  sigma = sigma,
                                  mu = mu)
plot(lineage_t,
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Trait value",
     type = "l",
     main = "Trait evolution in the time domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/trait-evolution-time-domain-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

Now let's see how this evolutionary process is expressed in the stratigraphic domain:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lineage_t |>
  admtools::time_to_strat(x = adm) |>
  plot(type = "l",
       xlab = "Trait value",
       ylab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
       main = "Trait evolution in the stratigraphic domain")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/trait-evolution-stratigraphic-domain-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

You can clearly see the jumps in trait value over gaps in the stratigraphic record, as all evolutionary history from within the gaps has been removed (punctuated equilibrium anyone?). If you would like to explore the effect of stratigraphy on trait evolution more interactively, have a look at [DarwinCAT](https://utrecht-university.shinyapps.io/DarwinCAT/), a shiny app that runs in your browser.

## Advance topics (optional)

### Correlation

Let's quickly dive into correlation using depth-depth curves. Depth-depth curves are very similar to age-depth model in the sense that they act as coordinate transformations. However, they translate data within the stratigraphic domain by associating coeval stratigraphic positions with each other.

We start by constructing a few more age-depth models:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
key1 = "proximal"
key2 = "midplatform"
key3 = "slope"
h1 = data_adm[,which(grepl(key1,names(data_adm)))] 
h2 = data_adm[,which(grepl(key2,names(data_adm)))] 
h3 = data_adm[,which(grepl(key3,names(data_adm)))] 
```
:::


With this, we can define the age-depth model object:


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
adm_proximal = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = t,
                          h = h1,
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")
adm_mid = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = t,
                          h = h2,
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")
adm_slope = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = t,
                          h = h3,
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")
```
:::


Now we can construct a depth-depth curve from two age-depth models using `adm_to_ddc`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ddc = admtools::adm_to_ddc(adm1 = adm_proximal,
                           adm2 = adm_slope)
plot(ddc,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Stratigraphic position proximal [m]",
     ylab = "Stratigraphic postion on slope [m]",
     main = "Depth-depth curve for correlation")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](adms_files/figure-html/construct-depth-depth-curve-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


This plot shows which stratigraphic positions in one section are associated with the other. The step-pattern is generated by gaps in the proximal section, as the slope accumulates sediment, even if the proximal section is subaerially exposed.

# Contributed variations

The sections below collect the changes made by the workshop groups in their own copies of this chapter (`adms_*.qmd`). Only differences in content and code are reported; purely cosmetic Markdown reformatting (bullet markers, blank lines around code blocks) is omitted. The code is shown but not executed, so it does not affect the output above.

## Martin Ruecklin, Richard Dearden, Myrthe van der Heide, David Cerny, Mark Patzkowsky

*(`adms_dc.qmd`)*

No changes to the text or code. The group added a header with their names and the comment:

> We just followed the tutorial to get a better sense fof what analyses are possible!

## Pedro Monarrez

*(`adms_pmm_mv-a.qmd`)*

Replaced the gradually doubling extinction rate in the last-occurrence example with a short, intense **extinction pulse**, and extended the figure to show the time and stratigraphic domains side by side.

Instead of an extinction rate that doubles linearly over the interval of observation, the rate is held at background level and multiplied 50-fold for 20 kyr starting at 0.5 Myr:

```r
n_lfo = 1000      # no of last occurrences
t_ext   = 0.50    # onset of the extinction pulse [Myr]
dur_ext = 0.02    # duration of the pulse [Myr]
bg_rate = 1       # background extinction rate (relative units)
mag_ext = 50      # pulse intensity as a multiple of background
d       = 1e-4    # tiny offset to make the step sharp

f_lo = approxfun(x = c(t_min, t_ext, t_ext + d,
                       t_ext + dur_ext, t_ext + dur_ext + d, t_max),
                 y = bg_rate * c(1, 1, mag_ext, mag_ext, 1, 1),
                 rule = 2)

last_occ = StratPal::p3_var_rate(x = f_lo,
                                 from = t_min,
                                 to = t_max,
                                 n = n_lfo,
                                 f_max = bg_rate * mag_ext)  # must be >= max(f_lo)
```

The rate curve is then evaluated on a fine grid (5000 points) rather than on the model time steps `t`, so that the sharp pulse is not missed, and the three panels (rate, last occurrences in the time domain, last occurrences in the stratigraphic domain) are plotted together with the pulse interval marked in red. The histograms use 60 instead of 30 breaks:

```r
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

t_fine = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 5000)

plot(x = t_fine,
     y = f_lo(t_fine),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Extinction rate [relative]",
     main = "Extinction rate",
     ylim = c(0, bg_rate * mag_ext))

hist(last_occ,
     breaks = seq(t_min, t_max, length.out = 60),
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Last occurrences",
     main = "Last occurrences (time domain)")
abline(v = c(t_ext, t_ext + dur_ext), col = "red", lty = 2)  # mark the pulse

last_occ_strat = admtools::time_to_strat(last_occ, x = adm, destructive = FALSE)
hist(last_occ_strat,
     breaks = seq(h_min, h_max, length.out = 60),
     xlab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
     ylab = "Last occurrences",
     main = "Last occurrences (strat. domain)")
abline(v = admtools::time_to_strat(c(t_ext, t_ext + dur_ext), adm, destructive = FALSE),
       col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

This moves the transformation of last occurrences into the stratigraphic domain into the baseline chunk, so it happens in the same figure as the time-domain histogram.

## April, Joël, William, Johannes, Tim

*(`adms_tb.qmd`)*

Explored how the **temporal resolution of the tie points** affects the age-depth model, by keeping the full-resolution model alongside a coarsened one and comparing the two.

The full-resolution model is stored as `adm_init`, and `t` and `h` are then thinned to every 50th time step before `adm` is built from them:

```r
key = "proximal"

adm_init = admtools::tp_to_adm(t = data_adm[,which(grepl("Myr",names(data_adm)))],
                          h = data_adm[,which(grepl(key,names(data_adm)))],
                          T_unit = "Myr",
                          L_unit = "m")

steps <- seq(1, length(data_adm[,which(grepl("Myr",names(data_adm)))]), 50)
t =  data_adm[,which(grepl("Myr",names(data_adm)))][steps] # time step
h = data_adm[,which(grepl(key,names(data_adm)))][steps] # heights at the location with key in the name
```

The plotting ranges are taken from the full-resolution model `adm_init`, and both sediment accumulation plots show the full-resolution curve in black with the coarsened curve overplotted in dark red:

```r
# constants for convenience
t_min = admtools::min_time(adm_init)
t_max = admtools::max_time(adm_init)
h_min = admtools::min_height(adm_init)
h_max = admtools::max_height(adm_init)
t_step = 0.01 # 10 kyr resolution

h_vals = seq(h_min, h_max, by = h_step)
# Time domain plot
plot(x = t_vals,
     y = admtools::sed_rate_t(adm_init, t_vals),
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Time [Myr]",
     ylab = "Sediment accumulation rate [m/Myr]",
     main = "Sediment accumulation (Time domain)")
lines(x = t_vals,
     y = admtools::sed_rate_t(adm, t_vals),
     type = "l", col = "#800020")
# Stratigraphic domain plot
plot(x = admtools::sed_rate_l(adm_init, h_vals),
     y = h_vals,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "Sediment accumulation [m/Myr]",
     ylab = "Stratigraphic position [m]",
     main = "Sediment accumulation (Stratigraphic domain)")
lines(x = admtools::sed_rate_l(adm, h_vals),
```
